newsitem.title: LEBANON: Pope visit raises spirits of Lebanon Christians.
newsitem.headline: Pope visit raises spirits of Lebanon Christians.

text.p: Pope John Paul's triumphant weekend visit boosted the morale of Lebanon's frustrated Christians, but analysts said local church leaders would have to act fast if they were to reap any fruit from the visit.

The huge welcome the pope received as he preached a message of Moslem-Christian reconciliation, political and social justice and independence for Lebanon galvanised the country and astonished the Moslem majority.
But when the 32-hour visit ended, Moslems and Christians alike were left with the question of what practical impact John Paul's emotive mission would have on Lebanon's deeply divided society.
Some Moslem analysts doubted that any real change could take place before a Middle East peace settlement made possible the departure of Syrian and Israeli troops whose presence dominates the country.
"I don't think there is going to be any change in political, economic or social matters as a result of the visit," said a Sunni Moslem newspaper editor who asked not to be identified.
"Maybe on the social level people will start opening to each other, but it will be very slight."
Christian commentators emphasised the emotional impact of the visit that brought out hundreds of thousands of people to welcome the pope in scenes reminiscent of a rock star's progress.

"He has planted a great hope in the Lebanese conscience and awakened in us a joy that for a long time we thought had become taboo in this country of sadness," wrote Ghassan Tueni, a leading Christian personality, in the an-Nahar daily.

"The pope's speech (to young people at Harissa on Saturday) will be the beginning of Lebanon's resurrection if our youth continues in the solidarity and determination they expressed at Harissa," Henri Sfeir wrote in Nidaa al-Watan daily.

The pope mapped out the road for Christians to follow back into the mainstream of Lebanese life by telling them it was time to revive their community which has been confused and divided since the 1975-90 civil war.

He told them to build bridges to the Moslems and start participating fully in politics as a pre-requisite for helping to bring about major changes down the road for a more democratic, sovereign and independent Lebanon.
He also told them to recognise that they were Arabs and to seek a role in the Arab world rather that looking to the West for support as they have done for centuries.
Analysts said a major impact of the visit was to confirm Cardinal Nasrallah Sfeir, patriarch of the Maronite church, as the dominant Christian leader in political as well as religious matters.

Sfeir is a tough spokesman for Christian grievances but he is widely respected and a moderate compared with some Christian politicians who have boycotted political life since the war on the grounds that it is superficially democratic and wholly dominated by Syria.
The patriarch will now have a tough time deciding how to take advantage of the pope's visit, said Michael Young of the Lebanese Centre for Policy Studies, a Beirut think-tank.

"Sfeir is perfectly aware that the pope has gone now and something organisational must take place," he said. "The momentum has to be picked up. Sfeir and the church will have to act as soon as possible."
Sfeir and the bishops would first have to explain the pope's message and distribute it among ordinary Christians.

The patriarch should then reach out to moderate Christian politicians already active in political life or outside it and forge a loose council or front to represent the community in national affairs, Young said.
But to do that without losing support in his community he would need a hand from the pro-Syrian government.
"I think the patriarch will say 'Let's build bridges, but we need some confidence-building measures in exchange'," Young said.
These could include the government stepping up the pace of helping tens of thousands of people return to homes they lost during the war, action on human rights and possibly the release of prisoners.

More controversial issues, like a possible pardon for former Christian warlord Samir Geagea whose sentencing to three life terms on different murder counts has angered many Christians, would have to wait for progress on the political front, Young said.
